name: Adaptation of Agentic AI: A Survey of Post-Training, Memory, and Skills
venue: arXiv preprint (arXiv:2512.16301, cs.AI / cs.CL). Submitted 18 Dec 2025 (v1), last revised 9 Mar 2026 (v3). Semantic Scholar classifies it as JournalArticle/Review. No peer-reviewed venue identified as of the cutoff; the stable public artifact is the arXiv preprint.
authors_affiliation: Pengcheng Jiang, Jiacheng Lin, Zhiyi Shi (co-first authors), Zifeng Wang, Luxi He, Yichen Wu, Ming Zhong, Peiyang Song, Qizheng Zhang, Heng Wang, Xueqiang Xu, Hanwen Xu, Pengrui Han, Dylan Zhang, Jiashuo Sun, Chaoqi Yang, Kun Qian, Tian Wang, Changran Hu, Manling Li, Quanzheng Li, Hao Peng, Sheng Wang, Jingbo Shang, Chao Zhang, Jiaxuan You, Liyuan Liu, Pan Lu, Yu Zhang, Heng Ji, Yejin Choi, Dawn Song, Jimeng Sun, Jiawei Han (senior author, corresponding). Primary affiliation: University of Illinois Urbana-Champaign (UIUC); other affiliations span Stanford, Princeton, Harvard, UC Berkeley, Caltech, University of Washington, UCSD, Georgia Tech, Northwestern, Texas A&M (TAMU), MGH, Keiji AI, and Unity.
code_url: N/A (no official code repository; this is a survey/taxonomy paper, not a system. The arXiv listing has no associated GitHub/code link as of the cutoff.)
maintained_repo_url: N/A (no continuously-updated paper list / leaderboard repository identified for this survey as of the cutoff; arXiv v3 (9 Mar 2026) is the latest revision.)
task_domain: Survey of agentic AI adaptation spanning multiple task domains: tool-use, retrieval/RAG, planning, code/software development, web/computer use, QA/multi-hop reasoning, embodied (Minecraft), and decision-making. Evaluation applications surveyed: deep research, software development, computer use, and drug discovery.
problem_setting: A survey (taxonomy/framework paper) that unifies post-training, retrieval, memory, and skill systems under a single notion of 'adaptation' (improving an agent, its tools, or their interaction after pretraining). It introduces a four-paradigm framework split by optimization target (agent vs. tool) and signal source: A1 (tool-execution-signaled agent adaptation), A2 (agent-output-signaled agent adaptation), T1 (agent-agnostic tool adaptation, including pre-trained reusable modules and 'graduated' subagents-as-tools), and T2 (agent-supervised tool adaptation, where a frozen agent's outputs supervise the training of memory systems, skill libraries, or lightweight subagents). Settings covered include offline SFT/off-policy and online/interactive RL (RLVR); single-agent and multi-agent/subagent pipelines; supervised, preference-based, and verifiable-reward signals. The survey situates adaptive memory and skill libraries primarily as T2 tool-adaptation mechanisms, contrasted with agent fine-tuning (A1/A2).
what_is_retrieved: As a survey, it catalogs what various adapted systems retrieve/store: memories (episodic/case-based, strategy-based, skill-based), skills (executable code, API/MCP protocols, programs, synthesized tools), trajectories, distilled strategies/heuristics, guidelines/rules, documents (RAG), and tools/APIs. Memory and skills are framed as 'two facets of the same adaptation mechanism': memory provides the storage substrate; skills provide executable, composable content.
retrieval_grounding: HYBRID across the surveyed space. The survey explicitly distinguishes static/agent-agnostic stores (T1: pre-trained tools, classic RAG corpora, embedding models) from GROWING/agent-written memory and skill libraries (T2: dynamic memory stores, skill libraries curated by frozen-agent success/failure). It notes skill-based memory bridges T2 (agent-feedback-curated skill libraries) and T1 (pre-trained, agent-agnostic tool APIs).
completeness_vs_topk_objective: Not a single objective; the survey discusses both. For retrieval/RAG tools it references fixed top-k ranking and intrinsic ranking metrics (nDCG, Recall@K). It frames adaptation objectives more broadly as maximizing tool-execution quality (A1, e.g., retrieval scores/success rate) or holistic final-output utility (A2/T2), rather than committing to a single completeness-vs-topk objective.
cbr_cycle_coverage: N/A (survey). The survey does not implement a CBR cycle, but it characterizes the surveyed memory/skill systems using a closely analogous lifecycle: skill acquisition (learn) / representation (store) / invocation (retrieve+reuse) / refinement (revise/retain via reflection, RL, or sharing); and memory formation / evolution / retrieval. These map loosely onto Retrieve/Reuse/Revise/Retain across the works it reviews.
explicit_cbr_grounding: False. The survey does not explicitly frame itself as case-based reasoning and does not foreground Aamodt & Plaza / Kolodner CBR terminology. It uses 'case-based memory' (raw trajectory storage) as one abstraction level within an experiential-memory hierarchy (case-based / strategy-based / skill-based, borrowed from Hu et al.), and grounds memory taxonomy in cognitive-science / CoALA (Sumers et al.) rather than the CBR literature.
retrieval_unit: Surveys multiple granularities of the retrievable/stored unit: full trajectories (case-based memory), distilled strategies/heuristics/workflows (strategy-based memory), executable skills/programs/code snippets and API/MCP protocols (skill-based memory), documents and (query,document) pairs (RAG), tools/APIs, specialist subagents (subagent-as-tool), and (for RL-optimized memory) state/case representations used by a learned policy.
index_source: HYBRID/both. The survey contrasts static or offline-induced stores (T1 pre-trained modules; classic RAG corpora) with online/test-time-induced growing stores (T2 dynamic memory and skill libraries that the frozen agent writes during deployment, e.g., Voyager's growing skill library, ReasoningBank's test-time memory curation).
index_structure_topology: Surveys multiple topologies. For T2 dynamic memory stores it identifies three design families: (1) hierarchical/OS-inspired tiers with page-eviction/garbage-collection (MemGPT, MemoryOS); (2) reflection-based consolidation (Generative Agents, A-MEM); (3) graph/structured indices keyed by relational/semantic structure (HippoRAG, SHIMI). Skill libraries are indexed by natural-language descriptions (Voyager); RAG uses flat vector indices.
retriever_type: Surveys all types: BM25/sparse and dense retrievers (RAG/T1), learned/trained retrievers optimized under frozen-LM feedback (T2, e.g., REPLUG), LLM-as-retriever/agent-initiated retrieval, and similarity-based retrieval over skill/memory stores. As a survey it does not adopt a single retriever.
retriever_learning_signal: Surveys the full spectrum and emphasizes a shift from similarity-only to learned signals. T1 tools are trained agent-agnostically (off-the-shelf or pre-trained, e.g., SAM, AlphaFold2, dense retrievers). T2 tools are trained under frozen-agent supervision via: proxy signals (REPLUG's perplexity-reduction / KL alignment), structured preferences, downstream-task effectiveness (s3's Gain-Beyond-RAG), and RL/learned policies (PPO, GRPO, soft Q-learning) where the frozen agent's downstream success is the reward.
query_construction: Survey covers several: raw query (classic RAG), agent-generated/reformulated search queries (learned searchers like s3, Search-R1), task descriptions used to retrieve skills (Voyager indexes by NL skill descriptions), and reflective summaries used to retrieve experiential memory. No single canonical query construction is adopted.
query_granularity: Surveys both task-level (one-shot retrieval of relevant skills/memories at task start, e.g., skill-library lookup) and step/trajectory-level (per-step interleaved retrieval in interactive tool-use and search loops). The four-paradigm framework formalizes multi-turn tool use as iterated single-step interactions.
when_to_retrieve: Surveys one-shot and iterative/interactive retrieval. Interactive RL-based methods (A1/A2 with tools, T2 searchers) retrieve iteratively within multi-turn rollouts; skill/memory retrieval is typically invoked when a new task arrives and refined across steps. Active/adaptive triggering is discussed in the broader memory-utilization literature it cites.
retrieval_trigger_signal: Survey-level: no single trigger. It describes agent-initiated tool/memory calls within interactive loops, fixed-schedule retrieval in classic RAG, and reflection-driven consolidation/retrieval in memory systems. Trigger signals are discussed as part of the memory 'dynamics' axis (formation, evolution, retrieval) rather than prescribed.
reranking: Survey acknowledges reranking as a component in surveyed RAG/retrieval pipelines (it cites retrieval benchmarks reporting nDCG/Recall@K), but the survey itself does not propose a reranking method. No paradigm-specific reranking is mandated.
retrieved_context_refinement: Surveys multiple post-retrieval/processing operations: distillation of trajectories into strategies/skills (case->strategy->skill abstraction), reflective consolidation deciding what to retain, progressive/lazy context loading for skills (SKILL.md, MCP, progressive context loading per Xu and Yan), and pruning/forgetting in memory management. As a survey it describes rather than implements a single refinement pipeline.
how_retrieved_used: Surveys all uses: prompt augmentation (RAG, retrieved exemplars/guidelines), skill reuse (retrieve-and-compose executable skills, e.g., Voyager), case adaptation (experiential memory guiding future tasks), and training signal (frozen-agent feedback used to train T2 tools/retrievers/memory writers). It positions adaptive memory and skill libraries as adaptation mechanisms that are an alternative/complement to agent fine-tuning.
planning_integration: Survey covers a range: one-shot exemplars at plan time, per-step interleaved tool/retrieval calls inside interactive rollouts, plan-then-retrieve and retrieve-then-plan, hierarchical subtask decomposition (e.g., GITM/DEPS in embodied settings), and skill retrieval-and-composition within planning loops. Planner subagents themselves are framed as T2-adapted tools (e.g., AgentFlow's learned planner over a frozen backbone).
reasoning_search_interleaving_granularit: Surveys per-answer (A2 final-output evaluation), per-tool-call within a rollout (A1 tool-execution signals; multi-turn tool use), and per-step interleaving in interactive search/RL methods (Search-R1, s3). The four-paradigm formalism treats each tool invocation as a discrete interleaving point.
retrieved_item_representation: Surveys the surface forms injected/stored: raw trajectories (case-based), distilled strategies/heuristics/free-text workflows (strategy-based), executable programs/code/skills and API/MCP specifications (skill-based), structured notes, and parametric/latent memory. It explicitly organizes these along an abstraction continuum.
abstraction_level_of_retrieved_unit: Explicitly central axis. The survey adopts (from Hu et al.) a three-level experiential-memory hierarchy: case-based memory (raw trajectory), strategy-based memory (distilled workflows/heuristics), and skill-based memory (executable code/APIs/MCP). It also references the broader spectrum from raw trajectory to procedural skill to single demonstration/hint across the works reviewed.
noise_robustness_mechanism: Survey-level: discusses generalization and robustness as an evaluation dimension (Sec 7.3.2) and notes failure-aware curation (ReasoningBank extracting preventative lessons from failures) and counterfactual/controlled evaluation to isolate tool contribution. It does not propose a single noise-robustness mechanism; it surveys robustness as an open evaluation concern (benchmark saturation, metric validity, backbone dependence).
memory_type: Surveys all: episodic, skill-library, workflow/procedural, graph/structured, hierarchical/OS-inspired, parametric, and latent memory. It adopts a tripartite forms/functions/dynamics lens (Hu et al.) and CoALA's working/episodic/semantic/procedural memory decomposition. Skills are framed as procedural memory.
write_back: True (for the T2 memory/skill systems surveyed). The survey's defining T2 characterization is that a frozen agent's outputs/downstream performance supervise how a memory module writes, retrieves, reflects, and forgets, and skill libraries grow by storing successful (verified) programs/skills.
online_growth: Yes for the T2 dynamic-memory and skill-library systems surveyed (e.g., Voyager's growing skill library, ReasoningBank's test-time memory curation, dynamic procedural memory). The survey contrasts these growing/test-time-induced stores with frozen T1 pre-trained modules.
write_back_trigger: Surveys multiple triggers across systems: on-success only (Voyager stores verified successful programs), on-success-and-failure (ReasoningBank distills lessons from both successful and self-judged failed experiences; EXPEL extracts rules from success and failure), reflective consolidation (Generative Agents, A-MEM decide what to consolidate), and OS-style eviction/garbage-collection (MemGPT, MemoryOS). No single trigger is prescribed.
failure_experience_usage: Surveys both success-only and success+failure usage. It explicitly highlights ReasoningBank (distills generalizable reasoning strategies from successful AND self-judged failed experiences, extracting 'crucial preventative lessons') and EXPEL (extracts rules from success and failure) as advances over success-only/raw-trajectory storage.
memory_evolution_update: Surveys the full range as a 'dynamics'/update-policy axis: append-only (Voyager adds skills without modifying existing ones, avoiding catastrophic forgetting), reflective consolidation/refine (Generative Agents, A-MEM), delta/refine-overwrite via iterative refinement (Cao et al.'s dynamic procedural memory; RL-optimized memory), and forget/prune via eviction or garbage-collection (MemGPT, MemoryOS).
retrieval_as_learned_policy: Surveys this explicitly as a distinct T2 trend. It tabulates RL-optimized memory/tool policies including Memento (M-MDP / Q-function via soft Q-learning, GPT-4.1 frozen agent), Mem-alpha (GRPO), MAE (REINFORCE++), AgentFlow (Flow-GRPO planner), Advisor Models, QAgent, AI-SearchPlanner (PPO), and s3 (learned searcher via Gain-Beyond-RAG) -- contrasted with fixed similarity top-k retrieval.
cross_agent_or_cross_framework_sharing: Surveys both. It notes community-shared/collective skills (SkillWeaver's community-shared API-level skills; agent skills as shareable, executable artifacts via SKILL.md/MCP per Xu and Yan; 'Agent Skills in the Wild' marketplace audit), alongside single-agent private memory. Co-adaptation and collective sharing are flagged as open problems (Sec 9).
benchmarks: Survey catalogs many benchmarks mapped to A1/A2/T1/T2. A1 (verifiable tool execution): HumanEval, MBPP, LiveCodeBench, SWE-Bench, MTEB Retrieval. A2 (agent final output): multi-hop QA (as used by Search-R1, ReSearch), GSM8K, GPQA Diamond, IFEval, Arena-Hard, GAIA, AgentBench. T1: MTEB / standalone retriever and model evaluations. T2 (memory/skill): LongMemEval, Skill-Inject, Agent Skills in the Wild. Integrated/long-horizon agent environments: WebArena, and others (Mind2Web/Online-Mind2Web, ALFWorld, ScienceWorld, Minecraft per surveyed systems). Application domains: deep research, software development, computer use, drug discovery.
benchmark_family: QA / multi-hop (GSM8K, GPQA, multi-hop QA); code (HumanEval, MBPP, LiveCodeBench, SWE-Bench); retrieval/embedding (MTEB Retrieval); web (WebArena, Mind2Web/Online-Mind2Web); embodied (Minecraft/Voyager, ALFWorld, ScienceWorld); tool/agent (GAIA, AgentBench); memory (LongMemEval); instruction-following/chat (IFEval, Arena-Hard); skill-security (Skill-Inject, Agent Skills in the Wild).
baselines: N/A as a survey (it does not run experiments with baselines). Instead it cites cross-paradigm empirical comparisons drawn from the surveyed papers, e.g., Search-R1 (A2) vs. s3 (T2) on RAG/QA, and DeepRetrieval's recall gains as A1 illustrations. The compared 'methods' are the surveyed systems themselves organized under A1/A2/T1/T2.
key_metrics: Survey distinguishes verifiable execution metrics (A1 & T1: pass@k, test-suite pass rate, retrieval Recall@K / nDCG, SQL correctness, formal-proof verification) from holistic utility metrics (A2 & T2: final-answer accuracy, win rate, GAIA score, task success rate of the frozen agent). It also emphasizes adaptation-dynamics metrics (sample/interaction efficiency, generalization/robustness, continual/co-adaptation stability) and systemic metrics (cost/inference-time compute, safety, alignment).
headline_result: Survey (no single experimental headline). Its most-cited illustrative comparison: in the RAG/QA case study, the T2 approach s3 trains only a lightweight ~7B searcher with frozen-generator feedback using ~2.4k training samples to reach 58.9% average accuracy (and 76.6% on specialized medical QA), comparable to or exceeding the A2 approach Search-R1 (~170k examples; 71.8% on medical QA) -- presented as evidence that T2's narrower optimization target yields high data efficiency, with explicit caveats that this is not a controlled comparison.
ablations: N/A as a survey (no controlled ablations of its own). It instead performs comparative analysis across paradigms (A1 vs A2; T1 vs T2; A2 vs T2 data-efficiency synthesis) and uses the Search-R1 vs s3 contrast as a quasi-ablation of optimization target, while explicitly noting confounds (backbone composition, training-data distribution, architecture) that prevent attributing the efficiency gap to paradigm choice alone.
evaluation_decoupling: Yes -- a central methodological point. The survey argues A1/T1 verifiable-execution metrics (intrinsic, e.g., Recall@K, pass@k) should be reported separately from A2/T2 holistic end-to-end metrics, and exposes the 'A1-A2 evaluation gap' (high recall but low synthesis, or high final accuracy with shortcut reasoning) to motivate decoupled, both-family evaluation.
process_vs_outcome_metrics: Survey advocates evaluating both. Beyond final outcomes it calls for process/dynamics metrics: sample and interaction efficiency, generalization and robustness, continual/co-adaptation stability, and intermediate skill-lifecycle quality (whether a skill library improves through reuse or degrades through drift) -- noting no current T2 benchmark measures these intermediate stages.
cost_efficiency_tradeoff: Explicitly treated (Sec 6.4, 7.4.1). It contrasts A2's monolithic, high-compute retraining (~170k examples for Search-R1) with T2's data efficiency (~2.4k samples for s3) and discusses cost and inference-time compute as a systemic evaluation axis. Trade-offs across paradigms (cost, flexibility, generalization, catastrophic forgetting, orchestration complexity, error compounding) are a core comparison theme.
context_budget_and_selection_count: Survey-level: discusses progressive/lazy context loading for skills (SKILL.md, MCP, progressive context loading per Xu and Yan) and hierarchical memory tiering (working vs. long-term, page-eviction in MemGPT/MemoryOS) as mechanisms to manage prompt/context budget. It does not prescribe a fixed k; it describes budget-management strategies across surveyed systems.
survey_scope_and_axes: Organizing axes: a four-paradigm framework split by (1) optimization target (agent vs. tool) and (2) signal source -- A1 (tool-execution-signaled agent adaptation), A2 (agent-output-signaled agent adaptation), T1 (agent-agnostic tool adaptation), T2 (agent-supervised tool adaptation) -- plus a complementary 2x2 design-space projection (monolithic<->modular on x-axis; local<->systemic orchestration on y-axis). Secondary axes for memory (forms/functions/dynamics; case/strategy/skill abstraction; CoALA memory types) and skills (granularity x acquisition mechanism). Coverage spans post-training (SFT/preference/RLVR), adaptive memory architectures, agent skills, evaluation, and four application domains (deep research, software development, computer use, drug discovery). Reference list contains on the order of 400+ citations (bibliography entries up to ~409); coverage window emphasizes foundational works through 2025-2026.
benchmark_construction_and_size: N/A (survey, not a benchmark). It catalogs and critiques existing benchmarks (Table of benchmarks mapped to A1/A2/T1/T2) and identifies a gap: dedicated T2 benchmarks that hold the agent fixed and measure marginal tool/memory value remain scarce; LongMemEval is highlighted as a dedicated memory benchmark testing five capabilities (information extraction, multi-session reasoning, temporal reasoning, knowledge updates, abstention).
builds_on: Builds on / synthesizes prior post-training and RL works (DeepSeek RLVR, Search-R1, ReSearch, s3, REPLUG, AgentFlow), memory surveys and frameworks (Hu et al. forms/functions/dynamics; Zhang et al. memory surveys; CoALA / Sumers et al.; Huang et al. foundation-agent memory), skill/procedural-memory works (Wu and Zhang; Xu and Yan; Fang et al.; Cao et al.; Voyager, JARVIS-1, EXPEL, Synapse, SkillWeaver, ASI, CREATOR, LATM, AgentStore), and dynamic memory stores (MemGPT, MemoryOS, Generative Agents, A-MEM, HippoRAG).
contrasts_with: Positions the four paradigms against one another: A1 (verifiable mechanistic mastery, expensive, poor cross-task transfer) vs. A2 (holistic orchestration, monolithic retraining, catastrophic forgetting) vs. T1 (agent-agnostic, reusable, possibly under-optimized for a host) vs. T2 (data-efficient modular tool/memory/skill adaptation under a frozen agent, bounded by backbone quality). It contrasts adaptive memory/skill libraries (mostly T2) as an alternative to agent fine-tuning (A1/A2), and contrasts narrower per-mechanism memory surveys with its broader adaptation-centric synthesis.
lineage: Surveys group. A unifying taxonomy/survey of agentic-AI adaptation that situates retrieval, adaptive memory, and skill libraries (T2 tool adaptation) alongside post-training (A1/A2 agent adaptation) and agent-agnostic tools (T1), bridging the RAG/retrieval, agent-memory, agent-skill, and RL post-training literatures under one 'adaptation' framework.
adaptation_mechanism: Core organizing concept. 'Adaptation' = improving an agent, its tools, or their interaction after pretraining. Mechanisms surveyed: agent adaptation via SFT, preference optimization, and RLVR (A1 tool-execution-signaled, A2 agent-output-signaled); tool adaptation via pre-trained agent-agnostic modules and graduated subagents-as-tools (T1) and via frozen-agent-supervised training of retrievers, memory writers, skill libraries, planners/advisors, and lightweight subagents (T2). The survey's distinctive claim is that adaptive memory and reusable skill libraries are themselves adaptation mechanisms (predominantly T2), complementary to fine-tuning.
tool_document_engineering: N/A (survey does not propose tool-description engineering). It does note skill/tool representation standards (SKILL.md, MCP protocols, API specifications) and progressive context loading as ways surveyed systems package tool/skill descriptions before invocation.
index_content_separation: Surveys this pattern: progressive/lazy context loading and SKILL.md/MCP interface standards (Xu and Yan) separate a lightweight skill index from heavy on-demand content; hierarchical/OS-inspired memory (MemGPT, MemoryOS) separates a small working context from large long-term storage with paging.
dynamic_index_and_protocol: Surveys MCP (Model Context Protocol) and function-calling as integration protocols for skills/tools, and discusses dynamic/growing skill libraries (live-updated by the frozen agent) vs. static pre-trained T1 modules. SKILL.md and MCP are highlighted as emerging interface standards.
tool_dependency_awareness: Surveys compositional skills (programs with loops/conditionals, e.g., ASI; compositional skill reuse in Voyager) and synthesized-tool maker/user pipelines (LATM, CREATOR), implying inter-tool/inter-skill composition, but does not center an explicit inter-tool dependency-graph model; this is treated lightly relative to memory/skill adaptation.
